reasoning:
**What is asked.** The 10-year Treasury constant-maturity yield (FRED series DGS10) for Friday 4 December 2026, in percent, as first published.

**Starting point.** The yield ended Friday 20 November at 4.92% on Treasury's figures (4.91% on Newsquawk's snapshot of 22 November), down 12 basis points on the day in a flight to safety as the S&P 500 lost 3.7%.

**What changed since my forecast of 22 November.** Part of that flight is unwinding. On Sunday evening S&P 500 futures were up 1.9% to 2.1% and Nasdaq-100 futures 2.6% to 2.9% (Bloomberg at 9:07 a.m. Tokyo on 23 November; Fortune, 22 November, 7:13 p.m. ET). Treasury futures fell in early Asian trading (Bloomberg) and a live quote put the 10-year near 4.95% (Investing.com, 23 November). Cash Treasuries do not trade in Asian hours today because Japan is closed. Treasury Secretary Bessent said on Sunday that the Fed risks a policy mistake if it overtightens, and traders pared bets on a December hike; that weighs on short yields more than on the 10-year. I move the centre up 3 basis points to 4.95% and keep the width.

**Width.** Nine and a half sessions remain (Thanksgiving closed, 27 November shortened). Daily moves of 8 to 9 basis points give a standard deviation of about 26 points by 4 December.

**What is scheduled.** A 2-year note auction on 23 November; the October PCE price index on 25 November, expected at 3.8% year on year (Bloomberg survey); ISM surveys in the first days of December; the November jobs report on the morning of 4 December, so the resolving value includes that day's reaction. The Fed decides on 9 December with a quarter-point hike still largely priced.

**What would move it.** A second wave of selling in shares would pull the yield toward 4.6% and take the hike out of the price. A rebound that holds would bring back 5.0% to 5.1%, and a strong jobs report could add to that.

**Forecast.** Median 4.95%; middle half 4.78% to 5.12%; 5th to 95th percentile 4.49% to 5.38%.
